articles.title: 5 Signs Your Thrift-Shop Furniture Find Is Actually Valuable—And a Great Deal
articles.content:
Few things compare to the thrill of finding a hidden gem at a thrift store. One minute, you’re browsing a jumble of junk, and the next, you’ve struck gold with a stunning vintage piece—at a fraction of what you’d pay for something new. Maybe it’s an Art Deco dresser with the coolest inlaid-wood waterfall design. Maybe it’s a curved Mid-century Modern sofa that looks like it belongs on a movie set. Or maybe it’s something a lot more modern that you just really, really love. Score! It can honestly be hard to believe that some of these items were given away. What were these people thinking?
Well, we’re glad they were thinking they’d donate these items instead of tossing them in the trash! Thrifting has skyrocketed in popularity lately, as shoppers look to save money and prioritize sustainable choices. And with more Baby Boomers downsizing, there’s a surge of well-made, older furniture finding its way into secondhand shops. In fact, people are calling this the Golden Age of Thrifting, and it’s exciting as it sounds—if you do it right. So how can you tell a true find from an old piece that’s simply seen better days? Knowing what to look for can help you spot quality craftsmanship, recognize furniture styles from different eras and avoid overpaying.
To uncover the secrets of buying secondhand furniture, we spoke with Danielle Sandusky, co-owner of Modern Bungalow, an award-winning furniture boutique known for American-made, Amish-built, solid-wood items. You’ll definitely want to read this before your next thrifting expedition!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more shopping, money, knowledge, humor, cleaning and fun facts all week long.
In many cases, older furniture was built with stronger, more substantial materials and better construction techniques than today’s mass-produced alternatives. There’s a good reason people say “They don’t make ’em like they used to.” However, age alone doesn’t guarantee quality. A well-made modern piece can be just as durable as a vintage one, and some older furniture was never particularly well made to begin with.
One reason older furniture can feel different is the way it was manufactured. Before large-scale industrial production became widespread, many furniture makers relied on skilled craftspeople and hands-on construction methods. Industrialization, of course, dramatically changed things with engineered wood, particleboard, laminates and other lower-cost materials. “Mass-produced furniture is carefully designed to look good in photos and from just one angle,” Sandusky explains. “If you start pulling out drawers and opening doors and it looks different than you expected, it’s because the company likely skimped on materials.”
Fortunately, quality craftsmanship hasn’t disappeared. There are still furniture makers producing solid-wood pieces with traditional joinery and durable construction. The key is learning to recognize those qualities, whether you’re shopping for something decades old or something brand new.
Before falling in love with a thrift-store find, take the time to examine how it was made. Here’s what can tell you more about an item’s quality than its appearance alone.
One of the easiest ways to get an initial sense of an item’s construction is to pick it up or gently test its stability. Solid hardwood furniture generally has some heft, while lightweight construction can indicate the use of thinner materials or hollow components. Sandusky also recommends pushing gently on a corner to see whether the entire piece wobbles. A sturdy dresser, table or cabinet shouldn’t feel like it’s about to come apart when you touch it.
For upholstered furniture, pay attention to the frame. Push down on the back and arms, and check whether they feel solid or hollow. If the frame bows, feels squishy or seems unstable, it may not have strong structural support. Alarm bells should also go off if you notice sagging cushions or wooden corners poking through the fabric.
The type of wood used in a piece of furniture can make a significant difference in its durability. Sandusky recommends familiarizing yourself with the grain patterns of hardwoods such as maple, cherry, oak and walnut. These denser, heavier woods are valued for their strength and appearance.
Look closely at the underside, back and edges of a piece to get a better idea what it’s made from. Can you identify the wood grain? Does the material look consistent throughout, or does it appear to be a thin decorative layer covering another material?
Sandusky suggests paying particular attention to the underside of wooden tables. A surface that is rough, unfinished or splintery may indicate that the maker didn’t put much care into the construction. You can also gently press a fingernail against an inconspicuous area to get a sense of the wood’s density.
Dovetail joints are one of the classic signs of quality furniture construction. These interlocking, wedge-shaped joints connect the sides of a drawer to its front and back, helping hold the pieces together without relying solely on nails or screws.
You’ll typically find dovetail joints at the corners of wooden drawers. They’re worth looking for in older furniture, particularly dressers, desks and cabinets. But don’t stop at the front of the drawer. Sandusky cautions that some manufacturers use dovetail joints only on the front corners to give the appearance of quality construction. Sneaky! So pull the drawer all the way out and inspect the back corners too.
Ideally, the drawer box should also be made from solid wood rather than plywood or another inexpensive material. These details can help distinguish a genuinely well-constructed piece from one designed to look more expensive than it is.
A manufacturer’s label, stamp, signature or other identifying mark can offer valuable clues about an item’s age and origin. Check the back, inside the drawers and even the bottom of cabinets for identifying information. A maker’s mark may help you determine who produced the furniture, when it was made and whether it belongs to a recognizable design collection. This can be especially useful when researching pieces from established furniture makers or well-known designers.
However, a missing label doesn’t automatically mean an older piece isn’t valuable. Many older furnishings were never marked, and identifying information can disappear over time. Think of a maker’s mark as a helpful starting point rather than a requirement.
Even a beautifully constructed piece can become a money pit if it needs extensive repairs. Before purchasing, inspect the furniture carefully, including areas that aren’t immediately visible. Watch out for structural damage, loose joints, water damage, warped wood, significant cracks and evidence of previous repairs. Check that drawers slide properly and cabinet doors open and close without difficulty.
The good news is that not every imperfection is a deal-breaker. Sandusky says surface scratches, worn hardware, sticky drawers and slightly crooked doors are often relatively easy to address. A little cleaning, a touch-up kit or replacement hardware may be all a piece needs. However, she warns shoppers not to underestimate the cost and difficulty of refinishing an entire piece of furniture. Stripping old finishes, repairing damaged wood and applying a new finish can require considerable time, skill and money.
When in doubt, distinguish between cosmetic imperfections and problems that affect the furniture’s structural integrity. The former may be an opportunity, while the latter could turn an inexpensive purchase into an expensive project.
Recognizing popular furniture styles can help you narrow down when a piece was made and what details to look for. Although styles sometimes overlap, certain materials, silhouettes and decorative elements are closely associated with particular periods.
Here are some of the major furniture eras and the features you might encounter while thrifting—or even find in your grandma’s attic.
One important distinction: A piece doesn’t have to belong to a famous design era to be worth purchasing. As Sandusky points out, the idea of collectible furniture can sometimes distract shoppers from what matters most when furnishing a home. “Collectible styles imply that you should expect it to grow in value,” she says. “That’s true for very iconic pieces, but for most of our homes, we generally aren’t looking to ‘collect.’ We simply want to furnish our lives.” In other words, don’t overlook a well-made, beautifully designed piece just because you can’t identify its exact era.
You don’t have to become an antique-furniture expert to make smarter thrift-store purchases. A few digital tools and reference resources can help you identify unfamiliar pieces and decide whether they’re worth a closer look.
A good deal isn’t necessarily the piece with the lowest price tag. Consider the quality of the furniture’s construction, its overall condition, the amount of work it needs and how much comparable pieces are actually selling for. Begin by comparing the asking price with similar items from the same maker, period or style. Look at completed sales rather than relying exclusively on current listings, since sellers can ask for just about anything for a vintage dresser or dining table.
Next, factor in the cost of any repairs or improvements. A sturdy wooden table with a few surface scratches may be an excellent purchase, especially if it only needs a little cleaning or polishing. But a piece with extensive water damage, broken structural joints or a finish that needs to be completely stripped and replaced may cost considerably more than its original price suggests.
Also keep in mind the furniture’s practical value. Will it fit in your home? Does it serve a purpose? Does it fit well with your existing furniture? Is it something you’ll enjoy using for years? A beautifully constructed piece that you’ll actually use may be a better investment in your home than an expensive collectible that doesn’t suit your needs.
And remember that resale value and personal value aren’t always the same thing. Even a piece that isn’t particularly rare or collectible can be worth purchasing if it’s well made, reasonably priced and you absolutely love it. Sandusky’s advice is refreshingly simple: “If it’s well made and makes your heart sing, grab it!”
Sandusky encourages shoppers to think about the experience of furnishing a home rather than approaching every purchase as an investment. “Don’t buy to flip,” she says. “Buy to make your home feel collected and cozy—full of the work of craftspeople grateful to you for giving their labor a second life.”
That’s perhaps the best part of shopping for secondhand furniture. You’re not just finding something to fill an empty corner. You’re giving a well-made piece another chapter and potentially bringing home something you’ll treasure for years to come.

articles.title: This Hidden iPhone Feature Will Make Holiday Cooking and Baking a Million Times Easier
articles.content:
Picture it: You’re making holiday cookies, up to your elbows in flour and sugar and little red and green sprinkles, when your recipe throws you for a loop. In the old days, you might have just muddled through and hoped for the best, or searched the back of your cookbook for tips and tricks to solve whatever problem you’d encountered.
But now, you’re more likely to reach for your iPhone, which is probably what you’re using to follow the recipe anyway. iPhones have changed the way we cook and bake, and I can’t tell you how many times I’ve reached for mine to Google something mid-recipe. But what if you didn’t have to search the internet at all?
Good news: You don’t, at least for one particularly common cooking problem—because the answer is right on your phone. Ahead, I’ll tell you about a super handy iPhone feature that I had no idea existed until recently but is guaranteed to make my holiday cooking and yours so much easier.
Read on to learn about this secret iPhone feature, and get baking!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, tech, travel, entertainment, humor and fun facts all week long.
It’s the Unit Conversion feature in your iPhone’s calculator, and it really helps. Need to know how many grams are in an ounce or how many pints there are in a quart? This little feature can tell you. Does your Nigella Lawson turkey recipe call for liters of brine instead of gallons? Grab your iPhone calculator and make that turkey with confidence.
I cook a lot, but aside from a handful of familiar conversions, like 3 teaspoons = 1 tablespoon, my brain just doesn’t have a lot of room for math-y minutiae. Just the other day, a recipe called for 8 tablespoons of water, and I got out a cup, filled it to the top and counted them out. Another wanted me to add a “dram” of flavoring, which might as well have been in a different language, not to mention from another century.
Little did I know that 8 tablespoons is a half-cup, and a dram is three-quarters of a teaspoon. You know what could have told me this? The Calculator app on my iPhone. If you’ve been using your calculator for years and wondering how on earth you missed this handy feature, it’s only been a thing since iOS 18 launched in 2024. So you haven’t been out of the loop for too long.
It’s easy, and you don’t need to download anything or update to a new version. Just follow these steps.
Yes! The Calculator also features a Math Notes section, which is similar to the regular Notes app but pulls double duty as a conversion calculator. Let’s say you want to make a note to yourself that 1 ounce equals roughly 28 grams. Click the Calculator icon in the upper right again, and this time, select Math Notes.
Give your note a heading, or just hit enter to start typing in the body of the Note. Type whatever you want to remember, such as “1 ounce to grams.” The Calculator will automatically convert it for you, as well as any other conversions you type, and keep a record of them for later.
Yes, and it’s kind of a big one. The Calculator conversion can’t convert weight to volume, which requires knowing the density of the product you’re measuring. In other words, it’s more math than a simple 1-to-1 conversion. So if you’re making bread and the recipe calls for 200 grams of flour, the Calculator converter will not give you the cups.
What it can do is convert weight to weight and volume to volume, as well as other measurements that share the same physical properties. But … you have your phone, right? One way to figure out how many cups of flour you need for that recipe is to use an ingredient-specific conversion chart, such as this one at King Arthur Baking Company.
Cooking conversions are a tiny sliver of what the Calculator can do. Need to change dollars to pesos for your upcoming trip to Puerto Vallarta? No problem. Running a 10K race and can’t remember how many miles that is? Pull up the Calculator. Other properties it can convert include energy (like calories to kilocalories), temperature (Celsius to Fahrenheit), time (minutes to hours) and tons of others.
Yes, but because Androids don’t have a single Calculator app like iPhones do, using it will depend on your device. On a Google Pixel, open the Calculator app and select “Unit Conversion.” Samsung Galaxy devices work the same way, but other Android devices may be slightly different. Keep in mind, though, that weight-to-volume limitations exist for both iPhones and Androids.

articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Give Someone a Gift They Can’t Return?
articles.content:
The only gift my grandmother ever gave me was a pair of used underwear she picked up at a garage sale. I was 12. I’d love to tell you I’m exaggerating for comic effect, but that’s just the kind of lady she was: frugal, practical and oblivious to other people’s feelings.
Sadly, my gift-related trauma doesn’t stop there. There was also the $20 spa gift card someone gave me as a “special treat.” As far as I could tell, nothing on that spa’s menu cost $20 (unless you count the cucumber water, and I’m betting that was extra), and I was too broke to cover the difference. So the card lived in my wallet like a tiny, laminated taunt until the spa went out of business, at which point I cried real tears over the $20 I had essentially set on fire.
But the Incident, with a capital I, is the one that still makes my jaw clench. When my husband and I got married, we received a gift in a box that said it was an electric teakettle. We didn’t need a teakettle, so we did the responsible adult thing and returned it, and we were thrilled to walk out with $75 that we promptly spent on stuff we actually needed. Victory! Adulting! Then, a week later, the store called. The box had not contained a teakettle. It had contained a cut-glass Easter basket. Someone had regifted it to us, tucked inside a teakettle box like a Trojan horse of tackiness, and the cut-glass Easter basket, I was informed, was not returnable. So we had to go back and hand the store $75 for the privilege of owning a huge, hideous basket that we then had to figure out what to do with. I am still bitter. (Yes, I’ve already complained about this basket on this very site, and no, time has not healed anything.)
I tell you this so you understand that I come to the question of nonreturnable gifts with a certain amount of lived experience. Because here’s the thing: We are constantly told to be smart shoppers. Start early! Hunt for deals! Stock up in July! But a lot of the best deals come with a catch. It’s final sale … or clearance … or thrifted … or from a charming little shop in another state … or bought so far in advance that the return window slammed shut around Labor Day.
So is it actually rude to hand someone a gift they can’t swap? I have thoughts. Several. Mostly emotional. Let’s dig in to the actual etiquette of this, my feelings aside.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, holidays, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Let’s start with the defense, because it’s stronger than you’d think.
First, a gift is a gift, not a lease. Somewhere along the way, we started treating the return option like a basic human right, right up there with running water and Wi-Fi. But for most of human history, people just handed each other stuff and the recipient said thank you. The exit ramp is a bonus, not a requirement.
Second, some of the best gifts are inherently nonreturnable. The hand-poured candle from the adorable shop in Vermont. The mug you found at a roadside stand. The sweater you grabbed at a price so low, you may have looked around for the hidden cameras. These gifts say “I saw this and thought of you” in a way that a shrink-wrapped, receipt-stapled whatever never will. Nobody has ever returned a souvenir. (And if they tried, the shop would be in Vermont.)
Third, and I want to be loud about this: Not everyone can afford to pay full price, and a gift giver should never be shamed for that. If the choice is between a clearance-rack scarf you can afford and nothing at all, the scarf is the generous, loving and perfectly polite option. Any etiquette rule that quietly requires you to spend more money isn’t an etiquette rule—it’s a tax. And the bottom line is that frugal is not a four-letter word.
Now for the prosecution, which is me, holding a cut-glass Easter basket.
A gift is supposed to make someone’s life a little better, not hand them a homework assignment. When you give something that can’t be returned, exchanged or swapped for the right size, you’ve placed a bet with their closet, their kitchen and their storage space, and they’re the ones who pay if you lose. They either keep it (hello, guilt!) or do the legwork of regifting, donating or reselling it, all while worrying you’ll find out. Meanwhile, you’re over here feeling virtuous about your $9 deal.
The sneakiest version of this is the giver who knows the gift is final sale and just crosses their fingers that nobody asks. That’s a game of Receipt Roulette, and the recipient never agreed to play.
It’s also worth remembering that for some people, the ability to return a gift has nothing to do with being picky. A returned gift can turn into groceries, a tank of gas or the thing they actually needed. A final-sale present may not look like a trap from the giver’s side, but it can feel exactly like one from the receiving end.
Welcome to the gray area. Population: all of us. These variables matter—here’s why.
So what about the deal-versus-safety-net question? If you’re torn between a pricier gift that can go back and a cheaper one that can’t, here’s my rule of thumb: For someone whose taste you know in your bones, grab the bargain. For someone whose taste is a mystery to you, pay for the safety net.
Do you announce “No returns!” when they unwrap it? No. Nobody wants a gift that comes with a legal disclaimer. “Enjoy! All sales final!” is not a sentiment you want written inside a card.
But if the recipient asks whether you have the receipt, you tell the truth, in one sentence, with a smile and an escape hatch: “It was final sale, so it’s yours forever, but if it’s not right, regift it, donate it or sell it. I will not be offended.” Asking for a gift receipt carries the same low-grade dread as getting a Venmo request for a $3 coffee, because suddenly everyone is doing math in front of a friend. Make it easy on them.
The truly rude move is the fib. “Oh, I must have lost it!” turns a bargain into a betrayal. And if you did get a gift receipt, tuck it in the box. That tiny slip of paper is the cheapest kindness in retail.
Thrifted gifts are having a moment, and the numbers suggest we’re a lot more open to receiving them than giving them. In a 2024 YouGov survey, three-quarters of 18- to 24-year-old U.K.-based respondents said they’d be happy to open a secondhand gift on Christmas morning, as would nearly half of people over 55. But when asked whether they’d actually buy a used present for someone else, most said no. A U.S. survey from the resale company thredUP (so take it with a grain of resale-flavored salt) found about two-thirds of Americans were open to receiving secondhand gifts as of 2021. So we’ll happily accept—we’re just squeamish about being the one who hands it over.
My take: Thrifted is fantastic when the secondhand-ness is the point. A vintage fondue pot that you hunted down for your fondue-obsessed friend? Thoughtful. A beautifully made wool coat in their exact size and color, which would cost $400 new? Genius. The rule is to clean it, package it with care, and for the love of all that is holy, make sure it’s not missing pieces or toting bedbug passengers. Used underwear remains, and I say this with experience, a hard no.
Is it really the thought that counts? Yes, but only if there was an actual thought, and not just “Oooh, $4.” I’ve ruled before that bringing store-bought food to a potluck isn’t rude, because showing up with some effort is what counts. Gifts work the same way. The price, the source and the packaging matter far less than whether you were paying attention to the person on the other end.
It is not rude to give someone a gift they can’t return. Clearance, thrifted, souvenir, final sale: all perfectly polite, and in many cases, the kindest thing a person on a budget can do. What is rude is the sneaking, the setting of traps and the getting weird about it afterward. So, in the spirit of the season, I give you three commandments:
1. Thou shalt not give a final-sale gift where size, shade or specs matter … unless you know them cold. Hand out the candles. Keep the leather boots on the returnable list.
2. Thou shalt tell the truth about the receipt. One sentence, no fibbing, plenty of grace.
3. Thou shalt not be offended by what happens next. Once it’s theirs, they can keep it, regift it or donate it. Gifts are freely given or they’re not gifts at all.
And if you absolutely must regift a cut-glass Easter basket, I beg you: Label the box honestly.

articles.title: Here’s the Real Reason Our Joints Crackle When We Wake Up in the Morning—And It’s Not (Always) About Age
articles.content:
One weird part of getting older is that at some point, it starts to take a little more effort to get going in the morning—and not just because we could probably use stand to hit the snooze button one more time. Our morning movements might become a little slower, a little more deliberate and even a little louder. Yep, that’s your ankles, knuckles, knees and necks crackling like a campfire.
Now, before you think I just called you ancient, some people just naturally have joints that crack as they move. My editor, for example, swears she was simply born that way and could never sneak up on her parents as a child, especially when walking down the stairs first thing in the morning.
So is this crackling OK, or is it a cause for concern? And why does it generally become more pronounced as we age? I spoke with Pamela Mehta, MD, a California-based orthopedic surgeon and sports medicine physician, to find out. Read on to learn the cause of those snaps, crackles and pops, as well as when they’re perfectly normal and when they could be a problem.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more health, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Very common! It even has a name: crepitus. (Which is a lot less awful than it sounds, I promise.) Crepitus can occur in virtually any body part with a joint, though it’s most common in the knees, shoulders, neck, ankles and knuckles, according to Dr. Mehta, who runs Resilience Orthopedics in San Jose, California. “You’ll hear it more in the first few movements you make in the morning because your joints feel stiffer after a night of not moving,” she explains. “Once you’re warmed up, this usually quiets down.”
Knee crepitus affects about 41% of the general population, but how often it occurs in other joints hasn’t been well established and isn’t as well researched. But we do know crepitus increases with age, since the lubricating cartilage between bony joints that keeps them moving smoothly (and quietly) wears away.
“It’s more common as we get older, because cartilage thins over time and your joints are stiffer and less elastic, so there is more for the joint to catch on,” Dr. Mehta says.
There are several possible reasons your joints sound like a bowl of Rice Krispies in the morning.
When we experience crepitus during our first movements of the morning, it’s usually because of gas in the synovial fluid. This fluid reduces friction between the bones in our joints.
“It’s often a tiny gas bubble releasing in the fluid that lubricates the joint,” Dr. Mehta says. “You can hear it, and you can sometimes feel it if you place your hand over the joint.”
When people have extra-flexible joints and a greater range of motion, they might experience more crepitus than others. “Muscle weakness or imbalances can also sometimes play a part,” Dr. Mehta says. “Many people find that the more they build balanced muscles around the joint, the less they notice it.”
As Dr. Mehta mentioned, the cracking in our joints tends to get more pronounced the older we get because our cartilage wears away and our joints get stiffer. “Arthritis is also more common as you age, and it can make the noise more noticeable,” Dr. Mehta says.
“A duller click or snap can be a tendon flicking over a bone, especially if it happens at the same point every time during a certain movement,” Dr. Mehta explains. Don’t worry—that kind of snap is usually normal and harmless. Tendons run close to bony points, and at a certain angle, a tendon can catch on the edge and then flick over it. The outside of the hip is common for this, especially when you swing out your leg or get up from a chair.
People who have osteoarthritis are more likely to experience crepitus (including 81% of people with knee arthritis), but the grinding or popping joints does not mean that you already have—or will someday definitely have—arthritis. “A grinding or or gravelly feeling, especially behind the kneecap, can be linked to changes in the cartilage,” Dr. Mehta says. “But it doesn’t always mean something is damaged.”
A previous injury to a joint makes it more likely that you’ll have crepitus in that spot. “You’re more likely to notice it in a joint you’ve injured before, such as a knee with a meniscus tear or a shoulder that has dislocated,” Dr. Mehta says.
Basically, yes, says Dr. Mehta. When we crack our knuckles, that satisfying pop we hear and feel is from the release of gas bubbles in the synovial fluid as the joint is stretched. “You’ll notice you can’t crack the same knuckle again right away,” she explains. “The gas needs time to dissolve back into the fluid.”
But the big difference between crepitus and knuckle-cracking is that crepitus is involuntary. Knuckle-cracking is a deliberate action we choose to take.
Luckily, those pops and cracks aren’t necessarily bad for your joints, even though they might sound like grinding gears on a manual transmission. Instead of worrying too much about how the joint sounds, pay attention to how the joints feel.
“If it doesn’t hurt, it’s usually nothing to worry about,” Dr. Mehta says. “The noise itself isn’t an issue. But if you feel pain, swelling or stiffness, especially if it’s getting worse over time, see an orthopedic doctor. I’d also want to see you if the joint locks, catches or gives way, or if this is a new thing that came on suddenly or after injury.”
It rarely requires emergency attention, but Dr. Mehta says to get care promptly if a joint becomes very swollen or if you can’t put weight on it after an injury. A hot, swollen joint with a fever, however, needs urgent care.
You might not be able to rid yourself of crepitus altogether, but it is possible to improve it. As long as those snaps, crackles and pops aren’t associated with any other symptoms, focusing on movement and strengthening your joints and muscles should help.
“Patients who build up their thigh and hip strength often find their knees feel better, even if the noise doesn’t fully go away,” Dr. Mehta says. “Strong muscles take pressure off the joint.”
You can do this with physical therapy, a strength-training routine in the gym, or bodyweight exercises (like squats and lunges) mixed with moderate cardio. Being at a healthy weight also takes the load off your knees and hips.

But we do know crepitus increases with age, since the lubricating cartilage between bony joints that keeps them moving smoothly (and quietly) wears away. 

“It’s more common as we get older, because cartilage thins over time and your joints are stiffer and less elastic, so there is more for the joint to catch on,” Dr. Mehta says. 

What causes this?

There are several possible reasons your joints sound like a bowl of Rice Krispies in the morning. 

Gas inside your joints

When we experience crepitus during our first movements of the morning, it’s usually because of gas in the synovial fluid. This fluid reduces friction between the bones in our joints.

“It’s often a tiny gas bubble releasing in the fluid that lubricates the joint,” Dr. Mehta says. “You can hear it, and you can sometimes feel it if you place your hand over the joint.”

Hypermobility

When people have extra-flexible joints and a greater range of motion, they might experience more crepitus than others. “Muscle weakness or imbalances can also sometimes play a part,” Dr. Mehta says. “Many people find that the more they build balanced muscles around the joint, the less they notice it.”

Age-related wear and tear

As Dr. Mehta mentioned, the cracking in our joints tends to get more pronounced the older we get because our cartilage wears away and our joints get stiffer. “Arthritis is also more common as you age, and it can make the noise more noticeable,” Dr. Mehta says.

Movement of ligaments or tendons

“A duller click or snap can be a tendon flicking over a bone, especially if it happens at the same point every time during a certain movement,” Dr. Mehta explains. Don’t worry—that kind of snap is usually normal and harmless. Tendons run close to bony points, and at a certain angle, a tendon can catch on the edge and then flick over it. The outside of the hip is common for this, especially when you swing out your leg or get up from a chair.

Osteoarthritis

People who have osteoarthritis are more likely to experience crepitus (including 81% of people with knee arthritis), but the grinding or popping joints does not mean that you already have—or will someday definitely have—arthritis. “A grinding or or gravelly feeling, especially behind the kneecap, can be linked to changes in the cartilage,” Dr. Mehta says. “But it doesn’t always mean something is damaged.” 

Injury

A previous injury to a joint makes it more likely that you’ll have crepitus in that spot. “You’re more likely to notice it in a joint you’ve injured before, such as a knee with a meniscus tear or a shoulder that has dislocated,” Dr. Mehta says.

Is this the same thing as cracking your knuckles?

Basically, yes, says Dr. Mehta. When we crack our knuckles, that satisfying pop we hear and feel is from the release of gas bubbles in the synovial fluid as the joint is stretched. “You’ll notice you can’t crack the same knuckle again right away,” she explains. “The gas needs time to dissolve back into the fluid.”

But the big difference between crepitus and knuckle-cracking is that crepitus is involuntary. Knuckle-cracking is a deliberate action we choose to take.

Is this bad for your joints?

Luckily, those pops and cracks aren’t necessarily bad for your joints, even though they might sound like grinding gears on a manual transmission. Instead of worrying too much about how the joint sounds, pay attention to how the joints feel.

“If it doesn’t hurt, it’s usually nothing to worry about,” Dr. Mehta says. “The noise itself isn’t an issue. But if you feel pain, swelling or stiffness, especially if it’s getting worse over time, see an orthopedic doctor. I’d also want to see you if the joint locks, catches or gives way, or if this is a new thing that came on suddenly or after injury.”

It rarely requires emergency attention, but Dr. Mehta says to get care promptly if a joint becomes very swollen or if you can’t put weight on it after an injury. A hot, swollen joint with a fever, however, needs urgent care.

Is there any way to get prevent this?

You might not be able to rid yourself of crepitus altogether, but it is possible to improve it. As long as those snaps, crackles and pops aren’t associated with any other symptoms, focusing on movement and strengthening your joints and muscles should help. 

“Patients who build up their thigh and hip strength often find their knees feel better, even if the noise doesn’t fully go away,” Dr. Mehta says. “Strong muscles take pressure off the joint.”

You can do this with physical therapy, a strength-training routine in the gym, or bodyweight exercises (like squats and lunges) mixed with moderate cardio. Being at a healthy weight also takes the load off your knees and hips.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Superman’s Rachel Brosnahan Reveals Her Family’s Hilarious Thanksgiving Tradition—And What She Hopes Is Next for Lois Lane
articles.content: Rachel Brosnahan knows a thing or two about playing strong, outspoken women. After winning an Emmy and two Golden Globes for her role as the quick-witted Midge Maisel in The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel, the actress traded stand-up comedy for superhero action, taking on the iconic role of Lois Lane in 2025’s Superman. And while she can certainly hold her own alongside the Man of Steel, Brosnahan has plenty of other things keeping her busy off-screen, especially with the holiday season right around the corner. In an exclusive interview with Reader’s Digest, Brosnahan gave us a peek into how she gets ready for the holidays, as well as the family traditions she looks forward to every year. She also revealed which of her famous on-screen characters she thinks would cause the most chaos at a holiday dinner party. (Spoiler alert: Midge Maisel would definitely keep things interesting.) But don’t worry, Superman fans: We didn’t forget about Lois Lane! Brosnahan also shared what it’s really like working with David Corenswet and what she hopes is next for her character in Man of Tomorrow, which hits theaters on July 9. And trust us—you’ll definitely want to hear what she has to say. Read to find out that and more. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. This interview took place on Oct. 27, 2026, and has been edited for length and clarity. Reader’s Digest: You’ve played so many memorable characters, from Midge Maisel to Lois Lane. If you could invite three characters you’ve portrayed to a holiday dinner, who would make the guest list, and who would bring the most drama? Rachel Brosnahan: Midge Maisel would bring the most drama for sure. She could come. She’d keep us all entertained. I would also invite Lois Lane. I feel like she would be very practical, and she’d make sure that we had everything we needed. I play a character named Eve in a film that will likely come out sometime next year called Saturn Return. I would invite her because she’s a deeply soulful person who I feel would bring some kind of conversation starter game and really bring the heart to the gathering. Reader’s Digest: You’ve partnered with Ferrero Rocher to celebrate the holidays and the brand’s new limited-edition cinnamon spice chocolate squares. What drew you to the collaboration, and how does its message connect with the way that you personally celebrate this festive season? Rachel Brosnahan: The holidays are made by the people that you spend it with. For me, I love the holidays. It’s my favorite time of year, and it’s such a wonderful opportunity to slow down and just spend quality time with friends and family, with your neighbors. And I feel like it’s the only time we ever get to all slow down together at the same time, and so I’m so grateful for that part of it. I’ve also been such a fan of Rocher for a long time. My dad used to bring back the trays of pralines from business trips, and they made me feel very fancy. It was a year-round thing in our household, not just for the holidays. But I have such fond memories of that particular flavor, and it’s been really fun to get to try some new ones that I hadn’t tried yet, like the new cinnamon flavors. I love dark chocolate, and it just feels like the holidays in a square. Reader’s Digest: I love how you talked about bringing the family together. Is there an unforgettable or hilarious moment from a holiday gathering that your family still talks about today? Rachel Brosnahan: I’ve been celebrating the holidays with my same group of extended family since I was a little kid, and it’s been such a beloved tradition. Thanksgiving is our holiday, so we’ve all grown up together and gone from being children to adults. Now we’re at a stage where everybody is of drinking age in the family, so we have started a beloved holiday tradition to find the drunkest cousin every Thanksgiving. Whoever ends up the drunkest cousin has to get up at the end of dinner and give a very heartfelt speech. Reader’s Digest: We’re so excited to see you return as Lois Lane in Man of Tomorrow. What is one thing about playing her that surprises you, and is there a side of Lois that you’re hoping to explore next? Rachel Brosnahan: I constantly get surprised when I get introduced, mostly by the fans, to different comics that I hadn’t seen before. I’m kind of a research nerd, and I did a a pretty extensive deep dive ahead of shooting the first film. But every so often, I’ll get tagged in something or DM’d a comic that I hadn’t seen before, and it’s just so fun to see different artists’ interpretations of the character and different adventures that she goes on. James Gunn, our wonderful writer and director, knows this, but I’m dying for Lois to fight some bad guys and do a little more flying—maybe in the next one. Reader’s Digest: What is it like working with your co-star David Corenswet, aka Superman? Rachel Brosnahan: He is one of the most incisive and smart actors I’ve ever had the privilege of working with. He really sees both the whole picture and also the tiniest detail at the same time, and he’s such a wonderful collaborator. This probably wouldn’t surprise people, but he’s an accent connoisseur. You can hear many different accents in a day coming from David. Reader’s Digest: For some people, The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel and Superman are comfort watches. Do you have a favorite comfort watch during Thanksgiving or Christmas? Rachel Brosnahan: I love the film Love Actually. We watch it every year. I also love Miracle on 42nd Street. The Holiday is another one! I love all the old holiday movies. We don’t have a physical TV in our apartment, so I miss being able to turn it on and let whatever movie is on play back-to-back for a week straight. It’s one of my favorite parts of the holidays that we’ve lost a bit in the digital age, but maybe we can recreate it in some way this year. Reader’s Digest: What’s an unpopular holiday opinion that you’re willing to defend, even if it might cause an argument at the dinner table? Rachel Brosnahan: I think my unpopular holiday opinion is that you can cancel your attendance to a holiday party last minute. It’s a crazy time for people. People are navigating so many different things, and I feel like people get very sensitive about last-minute cancellations to holiday parties. Reader’s Digest: If your family and your closest friends were asked to reveal one thing about you that would completely surprise your fans, what do you think they would say? Rachel Brosnahan: This is not new information, but it’s the first thing that comes to mind because I feel like people keep getting surprised by it. Before I ran around in skirts for a living, I was an athlete, and I was on my high school wrestling team. That remains a fairly surprising fact. Reader’s Digest: As you head into the new year, what are you most looking forward to? Rachel Brosnahan: I’m sitting on so many secret updates that I can’t yet share, but I have a number of different projects that will become clearer toward the end of this year and into early next year. I’m also looking forward to the holidays this year as an opportunity to slow down, catch my breath and reconnect with people. Reader’s Digest: Dogs or cats? Rachel Brosnahan: Dogs. Reader’s Digest: Mornings or nights? Rachel Brosnahan: Nights. Reader’s Digest: What’s your favorite book? Rachel Brosnahan: Right now, it’s Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking. Reader’s Digest: What advice would you give to your younger self? Rachel Brosnahan: Invest in Microsoft. Reader’s Digest: Would you rather travel to the past or the future? Rachel Brosnahan: The past. Reader’s Digest: If you weren’t an actress, what would you be doing?
